analysis.one_liner: Speeds environmental permitting, limits lawsuits over projects, and auto-approves permits when agencies miss deadlines.
analysis.headline: With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the National Environmental Policy Act to set strict deadlines for environmental reviews and permit decisions, with a potent backstop: if an agency misses its deadline, the permit is automatically approved. It caps environmental review documents, narrows the alternatives agencies must study, restricts public comment periods, and makes it much harder and costlier to sue over energy projects, including a rule that losing plaintiffs pay the other side's legal fees. It also requires approval of natural gas pipeline applications within one year, exempts many areas from Clean Air Act transportation checks, and gives permit applicants a 'bill of rights' telling agencies to seek favorable permit decisions.
analysis.who_benefits: Project sponsors and permit applicants — especially oil and gas pipeline companies, fossil fuel developers on public and Indian lands, and large infrastructure contractors — who would get faster, shorter environmental reviews, fewer agency objections, and approvals by default when agencies miss deadlines.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pipeline, oil, gas, and construction developers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a two-year deadline for environmental impact statements and a one-year deadline for environmental assessments, with extensions capped at one year or 180 days.
Provides that if a federal agency fails to act on a permit by its deadline, the permit is deemed approved and treated as a final, unreviewable-by-the-agency action.

Requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve or deny natural gas pipeline applications within one year, and other federal agencies to act within 90 days of the final environmental document, or their permits take effect automatically.

Limits most projects to one environmental impact statement and one assessment, allows agencies to adopt state-prepared documents, restricts cooperating agencies to comments within their own legal authority, and shortens comment periods to as little as 30 days.
Creates a 'permittee bill of rights' establishing federal policy that agencies should, to the maximum extent practicable, seek to issue permit decisions favorably.
Bars agencies from evaluating project alternatives the sponsor cannot feasibly carry out or that are not economically and technically feasible, narrowing the range of choices considered.

Requires energy-related lawsuits over permits on public or Indian lands to be filed within 60 days in a single district court and resolved within 180 days, and requires losing plaintiffs to pay defendants' legal fees unless their position was substantially justified; it also cuts off fee awards from the federal Judgment Fund to these plaintiffs.
Exempts transportation projects in areas classified as marginal nonattainment or attainment-maintenance from Clean Air Act conformity requirements.

Categorically excludes from environmental review repairs of structurally deficient roads, bridges, and transit facilities, and projects critical to communities imminently threatened by flooding or erosion.
Limits environmental documents to 300 pages without substantial justification, and lets only project proponents — not other members of the public — comment on any proposed exceedance of that limit.

analysis.who_pays: Communities near projects, people exposed to air pollution and contamination, and anyone who might use environmental review or courts to challenge a project. Weaker review, shorter comment windows, automatic approvals on missed deadlines, and fee-shifting against losing plaintiffs would reduce the public's ability to identify and stop harmful impacts before construction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near projects and citizen plaintiffs

drawbacks.text: Automatic approval of permits when an agency misses a deadline substitutes a paperwork clock for substantive judgment, meaning projects with real environmental problems could go forward because the agency ran out of time.

Sixty-day filing deadlines, mandatory fee awards against losing plaintiffs, and a single D.C. venue for energy-related lawsuits would make it substantially harder for citizens, tribes, and conservation groups to afford or bring challenges.
Narrowing the alternatives agencies must study and limiting cooperating agencies' comments reduces the analysis of routes, designs, and impacts before a project is approved.

An honest supporter would acknowledge NEPA reviews can drag on for years and delay needed infrastructure; the bill's categorical exclusion for repairing structurally deficient bridges and flood-threatened communities addresses that, but the same structure was used to fast-track pipelines and fossil fuel projects with far larger stakes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There are real delays in federal environmental review, and the bill's emergency-repair exclusions for flood- and erosion-threatened communities are sensible. But the bill's center of gravity is not targeted streamlining: it combines strict deadlines with automatic approval on missed deadlines, sharply restricted judicial review, fee-shifting against citizens who sue, and a policy presumption in favor of approving permits. That package mainly shifts power from the public review process to project sponsors, and the modest streamlining benefits do not offset the loss of the public's ability to examine and contest projects affecting their air, water, and land.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 20, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dan Sullivan (R-AK) introduced the Rebuild America Now Act on April 20, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No senator cosponsored the bill, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023; bills not enacted expire at the end of a Congress and must be reintroduced to advance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, current environmental review procedures, public comment rights, and access to courts remained unchanged. Communities that rely on environmental review and litigation to challenge projects are better off than they would have been under the bill; pipeline and fossil fuel developers who wanted faster permitting lost that opportunity.

for.name: Sen. Dan Sullivan
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alaska, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tom Carper (D-DE)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; it was sponsored by one Republican with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would require FERC to approve or deny pipeline applications within a year and would make other agencies' permits take effect automatically if they miss a 90-day deadline, sharply reducing environmental and agency review of pipeline routes and impacts.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and energy developers on public and tribal lands
industries.note: Short deadlines with default approval, one-review limits, restricted litigation (60-day window, single venue, fee-shifting) apply directly to energy projects on public and Indian lands, including Alaska Native corporation land.

Categorical exclusions for repairing structurally deficient roads and bridges and for flood- and erosion-threatened communities, plus expanded state authority over project approvals, would speed work contractors perform; this part runs alongside communities' interest in timely repairs.

Sixty-day filing deadlines, forced D.C. venue, 180-day resolution clocks, mandatory fee awards against losing plaintiffs, and cuts to fee funding would make challenges to energy and infrastructure projects far riskier and costlier to bring.
